questions.prompt: An EDM rule must match a US SSN and either the first name or email from the same indexed record. Which template logic expresses that requirement?

choices.text: Put all three columns in Any fields and require one match.
choices.feedback: This permits a lone name or email to trigger, which is weaker than intended.

choices.text: Place SSN in All fields and name/email in Any fields.
choices.feedback: The All group enforces the SSN; the Any group accepts either secondary identifier.

choices.text: Put all three columns in All fields and require every value.
choices.feedback: This rejects records where the SSN and only one secondary field are present.

choices.text: Create three independent DLP profiles and rely on policy order.
choices.feedback: Separate profiles do not express the required same-record conjunctive/disjunctive match.

questions.prompt: The EDM source is a locally uploaded CSV. The source file changed, but new records never trigger. What should be done?

choices.text: Increase the firewall policy session TTL so entries refresh.
choices.feedback: Session TTL does not refresh the EDM source or rebuild its indexed records.

choices.text: Change the DLP action from block to quarantine and back.
choices.feedback: Changing the action does not import the modified local data set.

choices.text: Restart the FortiGate so it rereads every uploaded file.
choices.feedback: A reboot is not the documented synchronization method for a local EDM upload.

choices.text: Use Update file to replace the local snapshot with the new CSV.
choices.feedback: Local uploads are not periodically synchronized; the administrator must update the file manually.

questions.prompt: HTTPS uploads reach the policy, but a known test record produces no EDM log. Which prerequisite is most important?

choices.text: Apply deep inspection and ensure clients trust the inspection CA.
choices.feedback: Encrypted HTTPS content must be decrypted before the DLP engine can inspect the matching fields.

choices.text: Enable only certificate inspection and trust the public website CA.
choices.feedback: Certificate inspection does not expose the HTTPS payload for EDM matching.

choices.text: Move the EDM template to the firewall address object list.
choices.feedback: Address objects select traffic; they do not enable payload decryption or DLP inspection.

choices.text: Set the policy to accept all traffic before the DLP profile.
choices.feedback: An accept action without the DLP profile does not create an inspection path.

questions.prompt: The EDM GUI lists a row as Valid, but a test value never matches its mapped type. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: The firewall has confirmed the record matched at least once.
choices.feedback: The entry list is not a match log and does not prove traffic matched.

choices.text: The policy is automatically blocking the value before logging it.
choices.feedback: A block action still produces DLP evidence when the inspected message matches.

choices.text: The GUI does not validate every row value against its column data type.
choices.feedback: A displayed Valid label is not proof that the value is usable for matching.

choices.text: The EDM source is refreshed only after a policy reinstall.
choices.feedback: Refresh and data-type validation are separate from reinstalling the firewall policy.

questions.prompt: A DLP log shows the EDM match, but the upload was allowed. Which object should be checked next?

choices.text: Check the DLP profile rule action and the firewall policy binding.
choices.feedback: The match proves detection; enforcement depends on the selected action and policy attachment.

choices.text: Change the external resource refresh interval to one minute.
choices.feedback: The source already matched; refreshing it does not change the profile's enforcement action.

choices.text: Replace the SSN data type with a generic keyword.
choices.feedback: Changing the type may reduce accuracy and does not explain an allow action.

choices.text: Disable deep inspection because the match already occurred.
choices.feedback: Removing inspection can stop encrypted content from being evaluated on later sessions.

questions.prompt: Remote Access returns a 502 after a FortiGate changes to a custom HTTPS admin port. What should be investigated first?

choices.text: Increase the ADOM database size and restart the policy install daemon.
choices.feedback: ADOM storage does not determine the FortiManager GUI proxy's upstream HTTPS listener.

choices.text: Check the upstream FortiGate certificate and custom admin-sport compatibility.
choices.feedback: The proxy must complete the upstream GUI transaction; a valid FGFM tunnel alone is insufficient.

choices.text: Reauthorize every managed device and regenerate its serial number.
choices.feedback: Device authorization does not correct an upstream GUI port or certificate mismatch.

choices.text: Disable the FortiGate administrator password and retry the redirect.
choices.feedback: The FortiGate still authenticates the administrator; removing credentials is not a proxy fix.

questions.prompt: The FGFM tunnel is established, but an operator's browser cannot open Remote Access. Which path remains unproven?

choices.text: The FortiGate's IPsec phase-two selector is negotiated.
choices.feedback: Remote GUI proxying does not depend on a branch IPsec selector negotiation.

choices.text: The ADOM's policy package checksum matches the FortiGate.
choices.feedback: Policy-package synchronization is separate from the browser's proxy connection.

choices.text: The FortiGate has learned every VLAN through LLDP.
choices.feedback: Layer-two neighbor discovery is unrelated to the Remote Access HTTP proxy leg.

choices.text: The workstation-to-FortiManager TCP/8082 proxy connection.
choices.feedback: FGFM verifies the management relationship, not the browser's access to the proxy listener.

questions.prompt: One administrator sees no Remote Access action while another can use it. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The managed FortiGate is in a different ADOM from the operator.
choices.feedback: ADOM placement alone does not grant or remove the explicit proxy capability.

choices.text: The FortiGate is using a dynamic IP address instead of a static one.
choices.feedback: Dynamic addressing does not explain a role-specific missing action in Device Manager.

choices.text: The first administrator's assigned admin profile lacks the proxy capability.
choices.feedback: The system proxy can be enabled globally while role-based permission still denies individual users.

choices.text: The operator's browser does not support the FGFM protocol.
choices.feedback: The browser connects to the FortiManager proxy; it does not implement FGFM.

questions.prompt: A customer uses FortiManager Cloud and asks for the same GUI Remote Access workflow. What is the supported distinction?

choices.text: GUI Remote Access is unsupported on FortiManager Cloud; SSH is separate.
choices.feedback: The Cloud limitation is specific to GUI proxy access and should not be generalized to SSH.

choices.text: Enable TCP/8082 on every Cloud tenant and the GUI proxy appears.
choices.feedback: Opening a port cannot add a feature that FortiManager Cloud does not support.

choices.text: Replace FGFM with SNMP polling to proxy the FortiGate GUI.
choices.feedback: SNMP polling cannot carry an interactive HTTPS administration session.

choices.text: Use the FortiAnalyzer report viewer as a browser proxy.
choices.feedback: FortiAnalyzer reporting is not a FortiManager managed-device GUI proxy.

questions.prompt: After a FortiAnalyzer reboot, Device Manager shows Down for 12 minutes while FortiGate says registered/up and receive counters rise. What is the best action?

choices.text: Immediately increase the no-log threshold to 24 hours.
choices.feedback: A temporary post-reboot lag does not justify hiding genuine logging outages.

choices.text: Delete and re-add the FortiGate in Device Manager.
choices.feedback: Re-registration is unnecessary when OFTP and receive counters already show recovery.

choices.text: Disable OFTP and force scheduled upload for every device.
choices.feedback: Changing logging mode introduces a different threshold and does not fix UI convergence.

choices.text: Allow the documented status convergence window, then refresh and recheck.
choices.feedback: The Community scenario describes a 10–15 minute UI lag while logs can already be arriving.

questions.prompt: A device uploads logs every four hours on a scheduled schedule. Which default no-log threshold applies?

choices.text: The near-real-time threshold of 15 minutes applies to all modes.
choices.feedback: The guide explicitly separates near-real-time and scheduled-upload no-log timers.

choices.text: The scheduled-upload threshold defaults to six hours.
choices.feedback: FortiAnalyzer maintains a separate threshold for scheduled uploads rather than using 15 minutes.

choices.text: The threshold is based only on the device's HA role.
choices.feedback: HA membership is displayed separately and does not replace the upload-mode timer.

choices.text: The status is always Up while the device is authorized.
choices.feedback: Authorization does not prove recent log receipt or an active OFTP connection.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly shows that FortiAnalyzer's OFTP receiver currently sees a FortiGate?

choices.text: The FortiGate policy hit count increases on the WAN interface.
choices.feedback: Policy hits show traffic forwarding, not delivery to the FortiAnalyzer log receiver.

choices.text: The FortiAnalyzer serial number appears in the inventory table.
choices.feedback: A serial number is static inventory data and does not prove current connectivity.

choices.text: The oftpd device listing together with increasing fortilogd receive rate.
choices.feedback: The listing identifies the session and the rising rate confirms incoming log traffic.

choices.text: The FortiGate displays a valid FortiAnalyzer address in its configuration.
choices.feedback: A configured destination does not prove a session or successful log receipt.

questions.prompt: A near-real-time device remains Down after 35 minutes, and no receive counters increase. What should be checked?

choices.text: Change the scheduled-upload threshold even though the device is real-time.
choices.feedback: The wrong timer will not repair the missing near-real-time log stream.

choices.text: Verify authorization, port 514 reachability and the fortilogd service.
choices.feedback: The delay is beyond the observed convergence window and receiver-side evidence is absent.

choices.text: Assume the GUI cache is stale because every reboot causes that.
choices.feedback: A persistent outage with no receive counters requires network and service investigation.

choices.text: Delete the ADOM and recreate it with the same name.
choices.feedback: An ADOM rebuild is not the first diagnostic step for missing device traffic.

questions.prompt: In dynamic-CAK MACsec, which sequence establishes the data-encryption key?

choices.text: LLDP creates the SAK, then DHCP supplies the CAK to the port.
choices.feedback: LLDP and DHCP are not the documented dynamic-CAK key derivation sequence.

choices.text: The PAE encrypts traffic with the RADIUS password before MKA starts.
choices.feedback: The RADIUS password is not used directly as the MACsec traffic key.

choices.text: RADIUS supplies MSK, CAK is derived, then MKA negotiates the SAK.
choices.feedback: The CAK supports key agreement; the SAK is the key used to protect frames.

choices.text: The FortiSwitch derives the SAK from its management IP address.
choices.feedback: The management address is not a source of MACsec session key material.

questions.prompt: A port is configured as a MACsec supplicant. What does that PAE role do?

choices.text: It requests authentication from RADIUS before the interface is allowed.
choices.feedback: The supplicant initiates the access request; the authenticator enforces the result.

choices.text: It acts as the RADIUS server and generates the MSK locally.
choices.feedback: The RADIUS server generates the MSK; the switch PAE participates in authentication.

choices.text: It bypasses RADIUS and uses the static PSK from the profile.
choices.feedback: PSK mode uses PAE none; dynamic CAK uses supplicant or authenticator roles.

choices.text: It disables MKA and sends all frames in clear text.
choices.feedback: Dynamic-CAK mode uses MKA to establish the secure association after authentication.

questions.prompt: RADIUS returns Access-Accept, but the Ethernet link never becomes MACsec-secure. Which layer should be checked?

choices.text: Change the switch management VLAN and clear the MAC address table.
choices.feedback: A management VLAN change does not establish the MACsec secure association.

choices.text: Increase the LLDP transmit interval to force key renegotiation.
choices.feedback: LLDP timing is not the control for MKA peer or SAK installation.

choices.text: Remove the MACsec profile and rely on the RADIUS server alone.
choices.feedback: RADIUS authentication supplies key material but does not replace the MACsec profile.

choices.text: Inspect MKA peer state, CAK agreement and SAK installation.
choices.feedback: Access-Accept proves authentication; it does not prove the MKA secure channel completed.

questions.prompt: A newly purchased FSR-108F supports MACsec in FortiSwitchOS 8.0. Which cipher limitation matters?

choices.text: The listed FSR-108F family supports only GCM-AES-128.
choices.feedback: The release notes specify this platform limitation; do not assume other ciphers work.

choices.text: Only AES-256-GCM is supported on the listed FSR models.
choices.feedback: That reverses the documented cipher limitation for the newly supported FSR models.

choices.text: MACsec is supported only in PSK mode on these FSR models.
choices.feedback: The release notes include both static PSK and dynamic-CAK support.

choices.text: The platform requires XPN with a 50-byte confidentiality offset.
choices.feedback: XPN and nonzero confidentiality offsets are not the documented requirement here.

questions.prompt: A FortiAP LoRaWAN gateway uses Basics Station. Which server handles configuration, certificates and firmware updates?

choices.text: The TC/LNS endpoint handles all firmware and certificate provisioning.
choices.feedback: That assigns the CUPS control-plane role to the traffic-controller endpoint.

choices.text: The FortiGate CAPWAP controller provides LoRaWAN sensor payload routing.
choices.feedback: CAPWAP manages the AP; the configured TC/LNS endpoint handles LoRaWAN data.

choices.text: The CUPS server handles provisioning and configuration updates.
choices.feedback: CUPS is the control/provisioning endpoint; TC/LNS handles LoRaWAN data traffic.

choices.text: The Wi-Fi DHCP server distributes the LoRaWAN gateway API key.
choices.feedback: DHCP does not replace the configured CUPS or TC authentication relationship.

questions.prompt: CUPS registration succeeds, but no sensor payload reaches the LoRaWAN network server. What should be checked next?

choices.text: Rebuild the FortiGate wireless SSID and change its WPA mode.
choices.feedback: Wi-Fi SSID authentication does not repair the separate LoRaWAN data endpoint.

choices.text: Verify the TC/LNS address, port, API key and selected gateway protocol.
choices.feedback: CUPS proves provisioning reachability; the TC/LNS path carries sensor data separately.

choices.text: Change the WTP profile name without changing the LoRaWAN profile.
choices.feedback: A profile name change does not correct the TC endpoint or credentials.

choices.text: Disable the CUPS server because it has already registered successfully.
choices.feedback: CUPS remains the configuration/update service and should not be removed.

questions.prompt: The LoRaWAN profile exists on FortiGate, but the AP reports no LoRaWAN configuration. What is the likely omission?

choices.text: The AP's client VLAN lacks an IPv6 default route.
choices.feedback: A client VLAN route does not explain an absent pushed LoRaWAN profile.

choices.text: The network server has not created a Wi-Fi SSID for sensors.
choices.feedback: LoRaWAN profile delivery is separate from WLAN SSID creation.

choices.text: The AP must first join a mesh root before receiving all profiles.
choices.feedback: Mesh root status is not a prerequisite in the documented LoRaWAN profile workflow.

choices.text: The LoRaWAN profile was not assigned to the AP's WTP profile.
choices.feedback: FortiGate pushes the LoRaWAN settings through the WTP profile binding.

questions.prompt: What does `cw_diag -c lw-config` prove when it displays EUI and CUPS/TC endpoints?

choices.text: It proves every sensor has joined and transmitted an uplink.
choices.feedback: Sensor association and payload delivery require separate server-side and radio evidence.

choices.text: It proves the AP has received the LoRaWAN configuration values.
choices.feedback: The output verifies pushed configuration, not successful CUPS registration or payload forwarding.

choices.text: It proves the LNS accepted the API key and stored every packet.
choices.feedback: The command displays local configuration, not remote LNS authentication or storage.

choices.text: It proves the Wi-Fi clients are using the LoRaWAN gateway radio.
choices.feedback: Wi-Fi client association is separate from the AP's LoRaWAN gateway function.

questions.prompt: Two groups match a host and assign different roles. How does FortiNAC resolve the conflict?

choices.text: The newest group membership always wins regardless of role ranking.
choices.feedback: The documentation specifies role order, not membership timestamp, as the precedence rule.

choices.text: The role with the longest name is selected to avoid ambiguity.
choices.feedback: Role names do not determine precedence; the Roles view order does.

choices.text: FortiNAC merges both roles into a combined policy automatically.
choices.feedback: The feature selects an effective role rather than combining multiple roles.

choices.text: The first matching role in the ordered Roles view takes precedence.
choices.feedback: The role list is ranked; the first matching role wins when multiple methods match.

questions.prompt: A user changes from Student to Faculty, but a host explicitly assigned Gaming remains Gaming. Why?

choices.text: The host has its own role and is not inheriting the user's previous role.
choices.feedback: FortiNAC updates inherited hosts; a distinct host-specific role is preserved.

choices.text: Directory synchronization never changes any host role after registration.
choices.feedback: Hosts that inherit the user's role can change when the user's role changes.

choices.text: The Gaming role is always higher than Faculty in every deployment.
choices.feedback: The example is about inheritance state, not a universal fixed rank for Gaming.

choices.text: The host is no longer associated with the user's account.
choices.feedback: A registered host can remain associated while retaining its explicitly assigned role.

questions.prompt: A host is removed from a group that assigned its role, but the old role remains. What is expected?

choices.text: The role should reset automatically after the next DHCP lease.
choices.feedback: DHCP lease renewal is not the documented role-reset mechanism.

choices.text: The host must be deleted and rediscovered to remove every group role.
choices.feedback: Deleting the host is unnecessary; the documented remediation is a manual role change.

choices.text: The role may remain and must be changed manually if a reset is desired.
choices.feedback: FortiNAC documents that group removal does not automatically clear the assigned host role.

choices.text: The directory server must send a RADIUS CoA for role removal.
choices.feedback: RADIUS CoA is not the documented mechanism for clearing this persistent role.

questions.prompt: A device is managed in Inventory and its role should place it in a VLAN. What else is required?

choices.text: A corresponding Network Device Role mapping must define the VLAN or CLI action.
choices.feedback: Inventory-managed devices need a Network Device Role to translate the role into enforcement.

choices.text: Only a user group is required because all roles directly configure VLANs.
choices.feedback: Roles and network-device mappings are separate configuration objects.

choices.text: A captive portal bookmark must be assigned to the switch.
choices.feedback: Portal pages do not substitute for a Network Device Role mapping.

choices.text: The host must inherit a user role before the switch can change VLANs.
choices.feedback: Inventory devices use the Network Device Role mapping, not user inheritance.

questions.prompt: A FortiNAC-F 7.6.3 system rejects an unsigned interim image before installation. What does that indicate?

choices.text: The runtime file-integrity monitor found a modified system file.
choices.feedback: An image signature rejection occurs during image validation, before the new image is installed.

choices.text: The signed-build upgrade guard rejected an image without trusted signatures.
choices.feedback: The signature check protects the upgrade path and rejects unsigned images by default.

choices.text: The appliance has lost its Internet connection to FortiGuard.
choices.feedback: FortiNAC-F performs signature verification locally and supports air-gapped environments.

choices.text: The HA peer is holding the firmware lock on the secondary node.
choices.feedback: The message concerns image authenticity, not necessarily HA ownership or synchronization.

questions.prompt: The NAC-F appliance is air-gapped. Can signed firmware verification still operate?

choices.text: No; each boot requires a live FortiGuard cloud signature lookup.
choices.feedback: The feature is explicitly designed to operate in air-gapped environments.

choices.text: Only if the administrator disables runtime file checks before boot.
choices.feedback: Disabling integrity checks is not a documented prerequisite for offline verification.

choices.text: Only after importing a new public key from the Internet every hour.
choices.feedback: The local trust material supports verification without hourly online key retrieval.

choices.text: Yes; the documented integrity and signature checks are self-contained.
choices.feedback: The release notes state that verification works without Internet access.

questions.prompt: A firmware upload passes signature validation, but a boot-critical file hash later differs. Which control detected this?

choices.text: The firmware download checksum alone detected the runtime change.
choices.feedback: A package checksum does not monitor files after the system is installed.

choices.text: The RADIUS server rejected the FortiNAC-F administrator.
choices.feedback: RADIUS authentication does not validate boot-critical file hashes.

choices.text: The boot/runtime file-integrity verification detected the installed-file mismatch.
choices.feedback: Image signature validation and installed-file hashing are separate integrity checks.

choices.text: The HA health check failed because the peer uses another version.
choices.feedback: HA version mismatch is separate from the runtime integrity check.

questions.prompt: A rollback to a pre-7.6.3 unsigned build is required. What does Fortinet document?

choices.text: The downgrade is possible with user confirmation, but returns to an unsigned build.
choices.feedback: The controlled downgrade path exists, but it changes the software trust posture.

choices.text: All downgrades are permanently blocked once a signed build is installed.
choices.feedback: The release notes explicitly allow downgrade to pre-7.6.3 unsigned builds with confirmation.

choices.text: The downgrade automatically retains signed-image enforcement on the old build.
choices.feedback: A pre-7.6.3 unsigned build does not provide the same signed-build protection.

choices.text: The administrator must enable Internet-based verification on every boot.
choices.feedback: The local verification model does not require an Internet connection.

questions.prompt: The default certificate policy is unchanged. What happens after a user PKCS#12 export?

choices.text: FortiAuthenticator revokes the user certificate and disables EAP-TLS.
choices.feedback: Private-key deletion is not certificate revocation; the certificate can remain active.

choices.text: The endpoint's private key is deleted when the browser closes.
choices.feedback: The policy affects the server-side generated key, not the downloaded endpoint copy.

choices.text: The certificate is moved into the Trusted CA store automatically.
choices.feedback: The export action does not change the certificate's issuer or trust-store location.

choices.text: FortiAuthenticator deletes its generated user private key after download.
choices.feedback: The default one-time delivery policy removes the server-side generated key after export.

questions.prompt: A user certificate remains Active after the FAC private key was deleted. Is that contradictory?

choices.text: Yes; a certificate cannot remain active without a server-side private key.
choices.feedback: The endpoint can hold the corresponding private key after it is downloaded.

choices.text: No; key deletion removes the server copy but does not revoke the certificate.
choices.feedback: Certificate status and private-key custody are separate lifecycle controls.

choices.text: Yes; the certificate must be deleted whenever a key is exported.
choices.feedback: The documented setting deletes the private key, not the certificate object.

choices.text: No; deleting the key automatically changes the certificate to Revoked.
choices.feedback: Revocation is a separate action and is not triggered by this policy setting.

questions.prompt: A deployment needs repeatable PKCS#12 exports for a staged endpoint rollout. What should be planned?

choices.text: Disable certificate expiration so the key can be downloaded again.
choices.feedback: Certificate expiry does not restore a private key deleted after the first export.

choices.text: Change the certificate's subject name and keep the same deleted key.
choices.feedback: Changing a subject does not recreate the missing private-key material.

choices.text: Use a controlled key-retention process or issue a new certificate/key pair.
choices.feedback: With deletion enabled, the original server-side key is not available for another export.

choices.text: Revoke the certificate and export its private key from the revocation list.
choices.feedback: A revocation list contains status information, not recoverable private keys.

questions.prompt: The browser reports a successful PKCS#12 download. What additional check proves the endpoint is ready for EAP-TLS?

choices.text: Confirm the FAC policy page still displays the default deletion setting.
choices.feedback: The policy state does not prove the endpoint imported the package.

choices.text: Verify the certificate and private key were imported into the intended endpoint store.
choices.feedback: A successful download proves transfer, not endpoint installation or correct certificate binding.

choices.text: Check only that the user's certificate serial number appears in FAC.
choices.feedback: The server-side certificate record does not prove the endpoint has its private key.

choices.text: Restart the RADIUS server and assume the endpoint enrollment succeeded.
choices.feedback: A service restart cannot validate local certificate-store contents.

questions.prompt: A template needs one credential to launch against several approved servers. Which field type is required?

choices.text: Add several ordinary Target Address fields to the same template.
choices.feedback: The documented feature is a dedicated field type, not duplicated standard fields.

choices.text: Use a URL field and store every server address in the password value.
choices.feedback: Credential fields should not be overloaded to bypass the target model.

choices.text: Use Multiple Target Address instead of the standard Service Address field.
choices.feedback: The 1.9 feature replaces the standard address field with a multi-destination allowlist.

choices.text: Create one secret per IP and link them to the same template.
choices.feedback: That duplicates secrets rather than using the supported single-secret multi-target feature.

questions.prompt: Which destination forms can the Multiple Target Address allowlist contain?

choices.text: IP ranges, CIDR networks, FQDNs and wildcard FQDNs.
choices.feedback: The documented allowlist supports both address ranges and DNS-based destination patterns.

choices.text: Only literal IPv4 addresses and TCP port numbers.
choices.feedback: The feature supports ranges, CIDR and FQDN patterns as well.

choices.text: Only DNS SRV records and URL paths with query strings.
choices.feedback: SRV records and URL paths are not the documented allowlist types.

choices.text: Only FortiGate address objects synchronized from FortiManager.
choices.feedback: The field is configured in FortiPAM target templates, not imported as firewall objects.

questions.prompt: A user selects a server outside the target allowlist. What should the launch workflow do?

choices.text: Allow the launch if the stored credential authenticates successfully.
choices.feedback: Authentication success does not authorize a destination outside the allowlist.

choices.text: Launch the session and log the mismatch after the connection ends.
choices.feedback: The destination constraint should be applied before the privileged session is opened.

choices.text: Automatically add the new address to the allowlist after the first login.
choices.feedback: Auto-expanding the allowlist would defeat the administrator-defined destination boundary.

choices.text: Reject or omit that destination because it is not an approved target.
choices.feedback: The allowlist constrains destination selection; it is not merely a convenience label.

questions.prompt: An administrator cannot find Multiple Target Address on an older FortiPAM build. What version boundary matters?

choices.text: The general feature requires FortiPAM 1.9.0 or later.
choices.feedback: The release notes specify 1.9.0 as the requirement for single secret to multiple targets.

choices.text: The feature is available in every 1.7 release if SSH is enabled.
choices.feedback: SSH availability does not add the 1.9 multiple-target template field.

choices.text: The feature requires FortiPAM 2.5 and a separate FortiSASE license.
choices.feedback: The documented version boundary is 1.9.0 and does not depend on FortiSASE.

choices.text: The feature is enabled only on FortiPAM Cloud and not appliances.
choices.feedback: The release notes describe the 1.9 feature without that Cloud-only restriction.

questions.prompt: A restricted OT Windows endpoint must send logs without registering to the Supervisor. Which deployment fits?

choices.text: Install a normal registered agent and set the Supervisor to offline mode.
choices.feedback: The standard agent still relies on Supervisor registration and management.

choices.text: Install a Linux osquery agent and forward Windows event logs over SNMP.
choices.feedback: Linux osquery does not collect the Windows Security logs on this endpoint.

choices.text: Use the Headless Windows Agent pointed directly at a Collector.
choices.feedback: Headless mode uses local configuration and uploads to the Collector without Supervisor registration.

choices.text: Send all Windows events directly to the FortiSIEM Supervisor over UDP/514.
choices.feedback: The documented headless agent path uploads to a Collector, not directly to Supervisor.

questions.prompt: How is the Headless Windows Agent licensed?

choices.text: It consumes no license because it is not registered to Supervisor.
choices.feedback: The release notes explicitly state that it consumes a device license.

choices.text: It consumes a device license, while events count toward EPS or GB/day.
choices.feedback: No Agent license is required, but the endpoint and event volume remain licensed.

choices.text: It consumes an Agent license but no device or event license.
choices.feedback: That reverses the documented licensing model for headless deployment.

choices.text: It consumes only a FortiClient EMS endpoint license.
choices.feedback: FortiClient EMS licensing is unrelated to FortiSIEM agent licensing.

questions.prompt: Which data sources are supported by the documented Headless Windows Agent configuration?

choices.text: Every registered-agent monitor type including WMI, osquery and discovery.
choices.feedback: The headless feature has a narrower supported source set than registered agents.

choices.text: Only Windows DNS and DHCP discovery application groups.
choices.feedback: Those groups are not the documented headless source limitation.

choices.text: Only packet captures from the endpoint network adapter.
choices.feedback: Packet capture is not the documented headless Windows Agent source type.

choices.text: Windows Security EventLog sources and user-defined log files.
choices.feedback: The installation guide limits exported headless templates to EventLog and user-defined files.

questions.prompt: A headless agent installs but cannot upload. Which Collector-side prerequisites matter?

choices.text: Enable IPv6-only mode and point the agent to the Supervisor address.
choices.feedback: The guide requires an IPv4-only Collector and Collector address for headless mode.

choices.text: Use an IPv4-only Collector, TLS 1.2 and valid Collector credentials.
choices.feedback: The agent uploads directly to the Collector and requires the documented TLS and IP conditions.

choices.text: Disable HTTPS and rely on the endpoint's local Windows firewall.
choices.feedback: The documented agent communication uses TLS 1.2 over HTTPS.

choices.text: Create an Agent Admin user only in the Supervisor CMDB.
choices.feedback: Headless upload uses Collector-side authentication rather than Supervisor registration credentials.

questions.prompt: Which combination is required before configuring agentless ZTNA bookmarks?

choices.text: FortiClient agent, EMS tags, a public SaaS URL and no proxy SSO.
choices.feedback: That describes a different endpoint posture/agent model, not agentless bookmark access.

choices.text: Only a browser bookmark and a public DNS record for the application.
choices.feedback: The bookmark alone does not create the authenticated SPA path to a private app.

choices.text: A FortiAnalyzer ADOM, a Collector and an HTTP syslog listener.
choices.feedback: Those components belong to log analytics and do not provide FortiSASE private access.

choices.text: Proxy, proxy SSO, licensed SPA hub and an HTTPS private application.
choices.feedback: The workflow depends on proxy identity, SPA routing and a supported HTTPS application behind FortiGate.

questions.prompt: Does the agentless endpoint need a proxy PAC file and FortiSASE deep-inspection CA just to open its bookmark?

choices.text: No; the bookmark flow uses proxy SSO but does not configure the endpoint as a proxy.
choices.feedback: Fortinet distinguishes proxy SSO configuration from endpoint proxy/PAC and CA requirements.

choices.text: Yes; every agentless endpoint must install a PAC file and CA certificate.
choices.feedback: The guide explicitly says endpoint proxy configuration and CA installation are not required.

choices.text: Yes; otherwise the browser cannot resolve the SPA hub's BGP route.
choices.feedback: BGP routing is handled by the SPA hub path, not by a browser PAC file.

choices.text: No; the endpoint bypasses all authentication and opens the private app anonymously.
choices.feedback: The user still authenticates through the configured proxy SSO provider.

questions.prompt: A private application is configured by FQDN behind a BGP-per-overlay SPA hub. What DNS setting matters?

choices.text: Set the DNS rule to Public so the browser queries its home resolver.
choices.feedback: A public DNS path may not resolve or reach the internal application namespace.

choices.text: Disable DNS and hard-code the user's home IP as the application address.
choices.feedback: The bookmark still needs the private application's name/address resolution.

choices.text: Set the corresponding internal DNS rule's Access Type to Private.
choices.feedback: The private DNS server must be reachable through the SPA path for FQDN application access.

choices.text: Use only the FortiSASE implicit DNS rule for every internal domain.
choices.feedback: Internal domains require the documented split/redirection rule and private access context.

questions.prompt: An endpoint has an active FortiClient agent/proxy session and cannot open an agentless bookmark. What is expected?

choices.text: Agent and proxy users cannot access the agentless ZTNA bookmarks.
choices.feedback: The feature deliberately separates the agentless bookmark flow from agent/proxy user sessions.

choices.text: The bookmark should work only after the user disables SAML SSO.
choices.feedback: The restriction is the endpoint session model, not a reason to disable SSO.

choices.text: The endpoint must be moved to a different ADOM in FortiAnalyzer.
choices.feedback: FortiAnalyzer ADOMs do not control FortiSASE bookmark eligibility.

choices.text: The FortiGate hub must be changed from BGP to static routing.
choices.feedback: The documented agentless workflow supports the specified SPA BGP designs.

questions.prompt: Which interface should be added as the SD-WAN member in the aggregate static IPsec design?

choices.text: Add each physical WAN port and remove the IPsec tunnel interfaces.
choices.feedback: That bypasses the documented aggregate IPsec logical interface.

choices.text: Add the logical ipsec-aggregate interface as one SD-WAN member.
choices.feedback: The Fortinet example uses the aggregate interface, not each tunnel as separate members.

choices.text: Add every Phase 1 tunnel as an independent SLA member only.
choices.feedback: That creates ordinary path selection rather than the aggregate per-packet design.

choices.text: Add the remote LAN interface as a local SD-WAN member.
choices.feedback: The remote LAN is not a local interface that can represent the tunnel aggregate.

questions.prompt: What is the main traffic behavior difference between this aggregate and ordinary session-based SD-WAN steering?

choices.text: The aggregate chooses a new BGP route for every Ethernet frame.
choices.feedback: BGP route selection is not the documented per-packet tunnel aggregation mechanism.

choices.text: The aggregate encrypts only the first packet and sends later packets clear.
choices.feedback: MACsec/IPsec encryption behavior is not replaced by packet distribution.

choices.text: Ordinary SD-WAN always fragments each session across every member.
choices.feedback: Ordinary SD-WAN steering is not equivalent to per-packet aggregate distribution.

choices.text: The aggregate can distribute packets from one stream across static IPsec members.
choices.feedback: Per-packet distribution differs from selecting one SD-WAN member for a session.

questions.prompt: Which command displays the configured aggregate IPsec members and algorithm?

choices.text: Use `diagnose wireless-controller wlac -c wtp` to list aggregate members.
choices.feedback: That command concerns wireless access points, not IPsec tunnel aggregation.

choices.text: Use `get router info bgp summary` to display all packet counters.
choices.feedback: BGP summary does not show the IPsec aggregate's member list or algorithm.

choices.text: Use `diagnose sys ipsec-aggregate list` on the FortiGate.
choices.feedback: The documented command displays the aggregate name, algorithm, member count and run tally.

choices.text: Use `diagnose switch macsec status` to inspect tunnel members.
choices.feedback: MACsec status applies to Ethernet link encryption, not IPsec aggregation.

questions.prompt: Both IPsec SAs are up, but only one aggregate member carries traffic. What should be checked?

choices.text: Confirm aggregate membership and that routing uses the logical aggregate.
choices.feedback: Established SAs do not prove that the aggregate is built or selected by SD-WAN.

choices.text: Change the Phase 1 proposal to a weaker cipher on both peers.
choices.feedback: A proposal change is not justified when both SAs are already established.

choices.text: Disable the second WAN interface so the aggregate has one member.
choices.feedback: Removing a member defeats the intended parallel tunnel distribution.

choices.text: Increase the FortiAnalyzer scheduled-upload threshold to six hours.
choices.feedback: Log upload timers do not affect IPsec aggregate forwarding.

questions.prompt: A per-packet aggregate performs worse when one ISP has much higher latency. Why?

choices.text: The aggregate automatically changes the remote gateway to the slowest ISP.
choices.feedback: The documented mechanism distributes packets; it does not rewrite the peer gateway.

choices.text: The second tunnel removes IPsec encryption from alternating packets.
choices.feedback: Every aggregate member remains an IPsec tunnel; encryption is not alternated off.

choices.text: The slow ISP prevents the RADIUS server from deriving a CAK.
choices.feedback: RADIUS-derived CAK belongs to MACsec, not static IPsec tunnel aggregation.

choices.text: Packets can arrive out of order and trigger retransmissions on latency-sensitive flows.
choices.feedback: Per-packet distribution exposes one stream to the delay variation of both paths.
